questions.stem: Which writ, whose Latin name literally translates to 'you may have the body', is issued by a court to secure the release of a person detained without legal justification?

options.option_text: Certiorari — quashes an illegal order of an inferior court
Habeas Corpus — produces the detained person before the court
Mandamus — commands a public authority to perform its legal duty
Quo Warranto — challenges a person's right to hold public office

questions.explanation: Habeas Corpus (B) means 'you may have the body' in Latin; a court issues it to compel the detaining authority to produce the detained person and justify the detention. Certiorari (A) is the tempting distractor but is used to quash an order already passed by an inferior court — a distinct purpose and stage.

questions.stem: Which Schedule of the Indian Constitution prescribes the forms of oaths and affirmations taken by the President, Governors, Ministers, Members of Parliament, and Judges?

options.option_text: Second Schedule — emoluments of the President and Governors
Third Schedule — forms of oaths and affirmations for offices
Fourth Schedule — allocation of seats to states in Rajya Sabha
Eighth Schedule — languages officially recognised by the Constitution

questions.explanation: The Third Schedule (B) contains the text of oaths and affirmations for constitutional functionaries. The Second Schedule (A) covers salaries, emoluments, and allowances — a common confusion with the Third. The Fourth Schedule deals with Rajya Sabha seat allocation, and the Eighth lists the 22 recognised languages.

questions.stem: A court has begun hearing a case that plainly falls outside its territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction. Which writ can a superior court issue to stop those proceedings before any final order is passed?

options.option_text: Certiorari, which quashes an order already passed by an inferior court
Prohibition, which prevents an inferior court from exceeding its jurisdiction
Mandamus, which directs a public body to perform a statutory legal duty
Habeas Corpus, which secures release of a person unlawfully detained

questions.explanation: Prohibition (B) is a preventive writ — it halts an inferior court or tribunal from proceeding further once excess of jurisdiction is apparent, before a final order is made. Certiorari (A) is the most tempting distractor: it is a curative writ issued after the court has already passed an order, to quash it. The two writs are complementary but apply at different stages.

questions.stem: The Ninth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, which shields certain Central and State Acts from judicial challenge under Fundamental Rights, was inserted by which Amendment Act?

options.option_text: First Amendment Act, 1951 — to protect agrarian and land reform laws
Fourth Amendment Act, 1955 — to expand state land acquisition powers
Twenty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1971 — to validate Parliament's amending power
Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976 — the sweeping 'mini-constitution' changes

questions.explanation: The Ninth Schedule was introduced by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 (A), along with Articles 31A and 31B, primarily to protect land reform laws from being struck down under Articles 14, 19, and 31. Candidates often confuse this with the Fourth Amendment (B), which extended the Ninth Schedule but did not create it.

questions.stem: Under Article 226, a High Court can issue writs not only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights but also for 'any other purpose'. Which among the following best captures this wider scope compared to Article 32?

options.option_text: Enforcement of Fundamental Rights only — the same scope as Article 32
Any legal right, including statutory and common-law rights beyond Fundamental Rights
Enforcement of Directive Principles of State Policy along with Fundamental Rights
Superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals within its jurisdiction

questions.explanation: Article 226 (B) gives High Courts broader writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court under Article 32; HCs can issue writs to enforce any legal right — statutory, common law, or contractual — not just Fundamental Rights. Article 32 is a Fundamental Right itself and is confined to FR enforcement. Option D (superintendence) describes Article 227, a different power.

questions.stem: The Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides for Autonomous District Councils to administer tribal areas. This Schedule currently applies to tribal areas in which set of states?

options.option_text: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram — the four states explicitly listed
All eight North-Eastern states, including Manipur, Nagaland, and Arunachal Pradesh
Only Assam and Meghalaya, where Autonomous District Councils were first created
Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya and Manipur as listed in Part B of the Schedule

questions.explanation: The Sixth Schedule (A) applies specifically and exclusively to tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. It empowers District Councils and Regional Councils to make laws on land, forests, and social customs. Manipur, Nagaland, and Arunachal Pradesh are covered by different constitutional provisions (e.g., Article 371A for Nagaland). Option C is a common misconception about its historical origin.

questions.stem: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 during an external emergency. Which distinct Article empowers the President to suspend, by a separate executive order, citizens' right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 for enforcement of other Fundamental Rights during a National Emergency?

options.option_text: Article 352 — which authorises the original proclamation of National Emergency
Article 358 — which auto-suspends Article 19 during an external emergency only
Article 359 — which enables a presidential order suspending the right to approach courts
Article 360 — which deals exclusively with proclamation of Financial Emergency

questions.explanation: Article 359 (C) is the mechanism by which the President can, by a separate order, suspend the right to move any court — including the Supreme Court under Article 32 — for enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights during a National Emergency. Crucially, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even under Article 359 (44th Amendment). Article 358 (B) is the tempting distractor: it operates automatically and only for external emergencies, suspending Article 19 alone, without any presidential order.
